description: We are the team behind Areographic, united by wonder and a shared curiosity about Mars. We bring NASA's open data into the choices a future explorer must make: where to go, what to observe, and when to return. Our approach combines scientific context, software and visual design, with human judgment at the center.
summary:
Areographic is a decision support service for potential biosignature observations on Mars. On a Marswalk, time, oxygen and radiation dose are scarce, so where a crew looks decides the science it brings back. Areographic answers the Martian Map challenge with a layered, integrated view of Jezero crater that helps a crew plan and carry out a Marswalk.

On the planning display in the habitat, spectral, geologic, thermal and topographic data (CRISM, USGS SIM 3464, THEMIS, HiRISE and CTX) become an exploration priority for 3,067 grid cells. Astronaut-safety limits exclude the sites a crew cannot reach and return from, and the planner sends the plan. On the helmet HUD, the astronaut matches a rover point-of-view image to the terrain, records six visual observations against a NASA reference image, collects a sample and decides when to return.

The records come back to the planner for the next plan. Each item is labelled as an observation, a published analysis, an estimate or a simulated value, every answer can be "can't tell", and nothing becomes a claim of life. It runs in a browser on open NASA data, with simulated mission telemetry and alerts.
details:
Target promising biosignature sites and reduce exploration risk.

[The problem]

  • On a Marswalk, time, oxygen and radiation dose are scarce. Where a crew spends them decides the science it brings back.
  • Jezero's ancient lake and delta deposits may preserve traces of past life. At Cheyava Falls, Perseverance found a potential biosignature. A biological origin remains unconfirmed.
  • NASA's Mars data is not layered for the small area a crew covers on one excursion, and Mars has no GPS. Planning and field observation have to stay connected.

[What it does: two views, one mission]

  • Planning display, inside the crew's habitat: rank sites, review the route, send the plan, receive the field report.
  • Helmet HUD, projected on the spacesuit's helmet visor: compare, observe, record, decide.
  • One shared mission: the same mission ID, plan version, route, task minutes and return budget on both.

[How it works: each NASA data layer changes a decision]

  • Where to go (spectral, geologic). CRISM mineral classes and the USGS geologic map SIM 3464 score every 160 m grid cell. Delta front ranks first with 84 points.
  • Where not to go (topographic). CTX terrain blocks slopes above 25°, and the return range locks sites the crew cannot come back from. Two of five candidate sites are excluded.
  • How to get there (thermal). THEMIS thermal inertia estimates rock cover, so the route map avoids rocky and steep ground.
  • What to look for (optical, with a chemical reference). The astronaut compares a Perseverance Hazcam view and the WATSON image PIA26368 with the terrain. The PIXL mineral map PIA26640 appears as published analysis.
  • Base map, route and 3D ground. NASA Mars Trek tiles, the Perseverance traverse and the HiRISE 1 m terrain model. Mars Trek and the Mars Perseverance Raw Images are resources the challenge lists.

⬇ How we use data: layer the evidence, convert ranks to weights, apply safety thresholds, recommend sites. Logo: AI-generated.

⬇ Planning display: candidate sites ranked by exploration priority. Two sites are excluded by the safety limits.

[A priority you can check]

  • Rank. The team ranks five indicators, informed by the iMOST report (2018). The current grid has data for the first two.
  • Weight. Rank-order centroid weights (Barron & Barrett, 1996): 45.7%, 25.7%, 15.7%, 9.0%, 4.0%.
  • Score. Exploration priority = Σ(w × S) ÷ Σw ÷ 4 × 100. Delta front: (0.457 × 3 + 0.257 × 4) ÷ 0.714 ÷ 4 × 100 = 84 points.

The planner can reorder the ranks, and all 3,067 cells are rescored at once. The priority is a team design that ranks where to look. It is not a NASA score or a probability of life.

[Astronaut safety comes first]

  • Return range. Four consumables with a 15% reserve set how far the crew can go.
  • Spacesuit mobility. A load-carriage metabolic model takes crew mass, carried equipment and slope, so heavier loads or steeper ground shorten the range.
  • Radiation and space weather. A dose budget per Marswalk, counted from the surface dose rate measured by Curiosity RAD. A simulated radiation storm, timed after the May 2024 solar activity, offers two responses: wait behind terrain, or stop tasks and return. No live space-weather feed is connected.
  • Communications. The planning display flags terrain-blocked radio shadow on the route. Field records are sent only while the link is up. After 10 seconds without it, the helmet HUD raises an alert and the planning display marks its last received status as stale.

These are prototype thresholds. The display does not certify a route as safe. The crew decides.

[In the field: compare, observe, record, decide]

  • Point-of-view match. Outlines traced from the rover's own image appear on the visor. The astronaut lines them up with the terrain and reports match or no match. Nothing is recognised automatically.
  • Six observations against the NASA reference image: layering, grains, sorting, veins, spots and a possible non-biological explanation. Each answer is Match, No match or Can't tell.
  • Sample. A mock collection at the estimated sampling point, with position, time and dose attached as simulated values.
  • Return. Acknowledging an alert, choosing to return and starting the return are three separate, recorded actions.

⬇ One task card, three buttons. The reference is the NASA WATSON image PIA26368 (archival).⬆ A mock sample at the estimated sampling point. HUD artwork: AI-generated.

[A worked example: Cheyava Falls]

One Marswalk to Cheyava Falls runs the whole loop in both views.

  • Plan out. When the planner leaves "Photo mark" out, the stay time moves from 20:00 to 18:00 and the turnaround time from T+25:00 to T+23:00, on both views.
  • Report back. The astronaut's answers, the sample record and the end report return under the same mission ID and stay in the archive for the next plan.

⬇ Why Cheyava Falls, and how each NASA item is used. The route is drawn at its Mars coordinates on the NASA Mars Trek base map.

⬇ The planner chooses the tasks; the return budget follows.

⬇ The helmet HUD receives the same plan version and numbers. HUD artwork: AI-generated.

⬇ Back at the planning display: the astronaut's answers, including "can't tell", and the end report.

[What is new]

  • One mission at two scales: a map for the planner and a short sequence of actions for the astronaut, kept in step.
  • Uncertainty is recorded: "can't tell" is a valid answer, and every item says whether it is observed, published, estimated or simulated.
  • A ranking you can argue with: change the order of the indicators and the map changes in front of you.

[Benefits]

  • For crews: more science from each Marswalk, inside limits they can see.
  • For scientists and planners: field observations that trace back to who saw what, where, and how sure they were.
  • For everyone: it runs in a browser on open NASA data, so anyone can plan and walk a Marswalk over real Jezero terrain.

[What we hope to achieve]

Show how open NASA data can support human surface science from the planning table to the helmet. Next: fill the remaining indicators, replace the prototype thresholds with validated models, connect live space-weather data, and evaluate the workflow with domain experts.

[What is built, what is simulated]

  • Built and running in the public demo: the planning display, the 3D field view with the helmet HUD, and the full Cheyava Falls loop. Other candidate sites run in a 2D simulator.
  • Simulated: mission clock, position, oxygen, radiation dose, vitals, the comm link, alerts and the sampling motion.
  • Fictional: the habitat, the crew rover and the spacesuit. The example route was driven by a rover and is not verified as safe for a walking astronaut.

[Tools]

JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js (WebGL), Leaflet and Vite, deployed on GitHub Pages. No server: the two views exchange messages inside one browser page.
